# Machine gun (`machine_gun`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs rifling_minie_breechloader; helped by smokeless_powder_high_explosive_shell, interchangeable_parts, machine_tools
- Core idea: An automatic machine gun uses energy from firing to continue its cycle. A hand-cranked Gatling gun depends on an operator turning the crank. Maxim demonstrated his automatic gun in the 1880s. Smokeless ammunition later reduced smoke and fouling. Early machine guns varied in weight and cooling system and required crews and substantial ammunition supplies. In the First World War they contributed to the strength of entrenched defences alongside artillery, fieldworks and wire.
- Pitfalls:
  - Hand-cranked multi-barrel guns (Gatling) are not automatic; the automatic principle is Maxim's
  - Without cooling the barrel overheats and wears out within minutes
  - Treating it as a kind of artillery placed far back, as armies did before 1914, instead of an infantry weapon firing across the front
  - It consumes ammunition by the cartload and so needs industrial supply
- History: europe: 1718 – Puckle's revolving flintlock gun, a curiosity; 1884 – Hiram Maxim's recoil-operated gun; 1914–1918 – dominates the battlefield; africa: 1898 – machine guns used at Omdurman in Sudan; americas: 1862 – Gatling's hand-cranked gun patented; east_asia: 1904–1905 – both sides use machine guns on a large scale in the Russo-Japanese War
- Read:
  - John Ellis, The Social History of the Machine Gun (1975)
